opus-5.5.text:
I think the first place people will feel it isn't in GDP numbers but in their own daily work. A lot of us already have a moment where we hand a task to a model and it comes back done, and done well, in minutes instead of days. At first it feels like a nice tool. Then one day you realize the bottleneck has moved. It's no longer "can I build this?" but "do I know what I want to build?"

For researchers and engineers it's already quite concrete. Things that used to need a small team, like writing infrastructure, running experiments, or debugging, can increasingly be driven by one person working with agents. So the unit of productivity shifts from the team to the individual plus their AI. I think that's the core of the explosion: the cost of execution drops dramatically, and what becomes scarce is taste, judgment, and the ability to ask the right question.

For ordinary people I suspect it will be uneven and a bit disorienting. Some will feel extremely empowered. Someone with an idea but no technical background can suddenly make an app, a film, or a small business. Others will feel anxious, because skills they spent years building become cheap overnight. Both feelings will be real at the same time.

And honestly, I don't think it will feel like one dramatic moment. It's more like boiling water. Each month the models get a bit better, and you adjust your workflow a bit. Then one day you look back and realize the way you worked two years ago is unimaginable now. The explosion is only obvious in hindsight.

What I hope is that people treat it as an expansion of what's possible rather than just a race to do the same things faster. If we only use AI to squeeze more output from the same old tasks, we miss the point. The real gain comes when people start attempting things they would never have dared try before.

r001.rationale: The response says people will hand tasks to models and that work once requiring a team can increasingly be driven by one person with agents, describing reduced need to do the execution themselves.

r002.rationale: It discusses changing skills, anxiety, and attempting new things, but does not recommend reconsidering what gives life meaning when work can be replaced.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people will feel it first not as a big-bang moment, but as a quiet shift in what they stop doing.

Take my own case. A year ago, if I wanted to understand a new paper, I'd read it line by line, take notes, maybe reproduce a piece of it. Now I throw it to the model, ask it to summarize the core idea, ask it where the weaknesses are, ask it to write a small experiment, and I'm done in maybe twenty minutes. The work that used to fill a whole afternoon now fills a coffee break. That's the productivity explosion. It's not that I became smarter. It's that the friction between "I want to know this" and "I know this" collapsed.

And once the friction collapses, people start asking for more. That's the part people underestimate. When something gets ten times cheaper, you don't just do the same amount for a tenth of the cost. You do a hundred times more of it. A person who could only afford to write one piece of software now writes ten. A researcher who could only run three experiments a week runs thirty. A small team starts doing what used to require a company.

So I'd say the experience goes in stages. First stage: the model is an assistant. You still drive, it helps with the parts you don't want to do. Second stage: the model is a colleague. You give it a goal, it comes back with a draft, you argue with it, it revises. Third stage, which I think we're entering now: the model is an agent. You describe the outcome, it goes and executes, and your job becomes judgment. Which problems are worth solving. Whether the result is actually right. What to do with it.

The honest part is that this will feel uncomfortable for a lot of people before it feels empowering. Because the skill that used to define you, whether it's writing code or writing documents, suddenly becomes commodity. What remains valuable is taste. Knowing what to ask for. Knowing when the answer is wrong. I think the people who adapt fastest will be the ones who are curious enough to keep pushing the model, and secure enough not to feel threatened by it.

So my answer is: you won't wake up one day and see the explosion. You'll look back after a year and realize you've been doing things you never could have done before, and you don't quite remember when it started.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the model now handles summarizing, critique, and experiment drafting, reducing work that filled an afternoon to a coffee break; later, it describes the model executing tasks while the person exercises judgment.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses changing skills and the value of taste and judgment, but does not recommend reconsidering what gives one's life meaning.

astra-6.text:
I think people will experience it first as a change in what they can accomplish on their own. Today, you might have an idea but lack the time or the skills to carry it out. As AI becomes more capable, you can describe what you want, work through it with the system, and get much closer to a finished result.

But doing individual tasks faster is only part of it. The bigger change comes when we reorganize work around those capabilities. If producing something takes minutes but getting it reviewed still takes weeks, the overall improvement is limited.

So I think the experience will be uneven at first. Some people will find that they can suddenly do work that previously required a whole team. For others, the change will be gradual. The real productivity explosion arrives when that ability becomes widely accessible—and when people have the judgment to decide what is worth doing with it.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI helping people accomplish more and do work that once required a team, but does not clearly say they will no longer need to perform much of their own work.

r002.rationale: The response does not recommend reconsidering what gives life meaning when much of one’s work can be replaced.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people will feel it first through the gap between having an idea and making it real. Today, even a simple idea can require learning tools, finding information, writing code, and coordinating with other people. AI can make many of those steps much faster. You describe what you want, work through a few iterations, and get something you can actually use.

But doing individual tasks faster is only the beginning. The bigger change comes when people reorganize their work around those capabilities. A small team can attempt projects that previously required a much larger organization. Someone with deep knowledge of a problem, but limited technical skills, can build a solution themselves.

That doesn’t mean productivity automatically increases everywhere. People still need to decide what matters, judge whether the result is good, and take responsibility for it. I think the explosion happens when the tools become reliable enough—and people become familiar enough with them—that using AI feels like a normal part of turning an intention into an outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says AI speeds up tasks and helps people build solutions, but does not identify needing to do much less of one’s work oneself as a direct experience of the productivity explosion.

r002.rationale: The response discusses deciding what matters and taking responsibility, but does not recommend reconsidering what gives life meaning when work can be replaced.
